nameStory: Bilimbia fuscoviridis gets its scientific name from Latin words meaning "dark green," which perfectly describes this lichen's distinctive coloration. The genus name Bilimbia honors early lichen researchers, though the exact origin is debated among botanists. Since this species lacks a widely-used common name, scientists simply refer to it by its scientific moniker.
description: Bilimbia fuscoviridis is a small, crusty lichen that forms thin patches on tree bark and occasionally rocks. It appears as a dark greenish-gray coating that can be easily overlooked among other bark-dwelling lichens. Individual patches rarely exceed a few inches across, creating subtle mottled patterns on its host surface. This inconspicuous lichen represents one of New England's rarest finds, with very few confirmed sightings.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark greenish-gray when moist, becoming more grayish when dry - like wet moss that's starting to fade

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Crustose (crusty) growth that forms thin, closely adhered patches on bark - feels slightly rough like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on smooth bark of deciduous trees, particularly preferring younger branches and trunks

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly granular surface with occasional small, dark fruiting bodies that look like tiny black dots

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Forms small colonies typically 1-3 inches across, though multiple patches may merge on favorable bark surfaces

habitat: This rare lichen inhabits the bark of deciduous trees in mature forests, particularly favoring areas with high humidity and filtered light. It's most likely to be found in sheltered woodland valleys and ravines where morning fog lingers. The few New England records suggest it prefers areas with consistent moisture but good air circulation.

seasonality.spring: Most visible when spring rains keep it consistently moist, showing its characteristic dark green coloration most clearly during frequent April showers.
seasonality.summer: May become less obvious during dry spells as it shifts to grayer tones, but morning dew often reveals its green hues in shaded forest locations.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture makes it more apparent again, and the absence of leaves provides better visibility on tree trunks and branches.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but often appears more grayish, though wet winter days can still bring out subtle green tones in this persistent species.

funFact: With only one confirmed observation in all of New England, finding Bilimbia fuscoviridis would be like discovering a botanical unicorn - you'd literally be looking at one of the region's rarest living organisms!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for other small, dark crustose lichens on bark, but its distinctive dark greenish color when moist sets it apart from most common bark lichens. Remember: if it looks genuinely green-tinged rather than gray or brown, you might have found something special.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertainty note**: Information about this extremely rare species is limited, and some identification details are based on general knowledge of similar lichens rather than extensive field observations of this specific species in New England.
compareHints: Bilimbia fuscoviridis differs from its relative Six-celled Moss Dot Lichen by preferring bark over soil or rock substrates and showing more pronounced green coloration when wet. While Six-celled Moss Dot Lichen typically grows on sandy or disturbed soil, this species sticks to tree bark in undisturbed forest settings. Both are small and crusty, but substrate preference is the key distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative Bilimbia fuscoviridis, Six-celled Moss Dot Lichen is more specialized for moss substrates and has smaller fruiting bodies.
